chapter.name: State and Society up to 1000 CE
chapter.blurb: Early Indian state and society: Vedic literature, political institutions, kingship and administration, ethics, social organisation, religion, education and the economy.

scope_in.item: Meaning of society and State; Vedic literature as a source
Janas, assemblies, janapadas, mahajanapadas, Magadha and the early kingdoms of the south
Ideas of kingship, saptanga, the pan-Indian ideal and the Junagadh inscription
Administration of kingdoms and empires, village assemblies and the Uttaramerur inscription
Ethics, samatva, rita and dharma and the link with politics
Varna, jati, family, ashramas, purusharthas and women
Religious life, Bhakti, education and knowledge traditions
Agriculture, irrigation, trade, ports and guilds

scope_out.item: Detailed history of individual dynasties and battles

scope_out.reason: Covered in later chapters and Part 2

scope_out.item: Detailed teachings of the Bhakti saints
scope_out.reason: The chapter says these come in Part 2

scope_out.item: India's trade with the wider world in detail
scope_out.reason: Covered in the chapter India and the World in Part 2

concepts.name: Society, State and the Vedic literature as a source
concepts.description: The meaning of society and State and the Vedic texts as the earliest literary source for early Indian state and society.
concepts.idea: A society is a system of relationships regulated by custom; a State is an organised political system based on rules and laws.
concepts.rule: Society: relationships among people sharing territory, culture and belonging, regulated by customs. State: organised political system with laws, rights and duties, and institutions for order. Each Veda has four parts: samhita, brahmana, aranyaka, upanishad. Rigveda earliest, composed in the northwest (Sapta-Sindhu).
concepts.example: The Rigveda was composed in the region where the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation flourished.

questions.q: A society is a system of social relationships among people who share
questions.a: a common territory, culture and sense of belonging
o: a common territory, culture and sense of belonging

questions.q: A State is
questions.a: an organised political system based on rules and laws
o: an organised political system based on rules and laws
a group of villages without rules

questions.q: The earliest known literary source of Indian literature is the ____.
questions.a: Rigveda

questions.q: Each text of the Veda has four parts:
questions.a: samhita, brahmana, aranyaka and upanishad

questions.q: Society is mainly regulated by
questions.a: customs and practices

questions.q: Vedic literature existed for many centuries in
questions.a: oral form before being written down
o: oral form before being written down

questions.q: The samhitas mainly contain
questions.a: hymns for invoking deities and offering praise
o: hymns for invoking deities and offering praise

questions.q: The Brahmanas are
questions.a: prose texts explaining rituals
o: texts of the forest hermits only

questions.q: Distinguish between the Aranyakas and the Upanishads and the samhitas.
questions.a: Samhitas are hymns invoking deities. Aranyakas (forest texts) expand on philosophical speculations of sages. Upanishads delve into deeper philosophical questions.
s: Aranyakas and Upanishads as philosophical texts

questions.q: The earliest sections of the Rigveda were composed in the region called
questions.a: Sapta-Sindhu

questions.q: Sapta-Sindhu includes the Indus River, its five tributaries and the ____.
questions.a: Sarasvati

questions.q: The date of composition of the Rigveda
questions.a: is debated, from the fifth to the second millennium BCE
o: is debated, from the fifth to the second millennium BCE

questions.q: Why are the Vedic texts important for historians?
questions.a: They show the times and places in which they were composed and give insights into people's lives, social structures, political systems, economic pursuits and religious practices.
s: Give insights into society, politics or religion

questions.q: What does the chapter say about the Rigveda and the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation?
questions.a: The Rigveda was composed in the northwest where the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation flourished. Since the Harappan script is undeciphered, the Vedas are the earliest known corpus of Indian literature.
s: Vedas the earliest literature as the script is undeciphered

questions.q: Explain the structure of a Veda and what each part contains.
questions.a: Each Veda has samhita (hymns), brahmana (prose explaining rituals), aranyaka (philosophical speculations of forest sages) and upanishad (deeper philosophical inquiry).

questions.q: Why are literary sources useful along with archaeological evidence from the second millennium BCE?
questions.a: They provide insights into social, political, cultural and moral dimensions
o: They provide insights into social, political, cultural and moral dimensions

questions.q: Distinguish Brahman, Brahmanas and Brahmins.
questions.a: Brahman is a concept (the ultimate reality), Brahmanas are texts explaining rituals, and Brahmins are people (a social group).
s: Brahmanas as texts and Brahmins as people

questions.q: Explain how the Vedas are regarded as foundational to Indian culture.
questions.a: They are one of the earliest texts, describe the times, places, society, politics, economy and religion of their age, and many cultural practices continued, so they form a foundation of Indian culture and traditions.

questions.q: Ravi says the Vedas were written down at the time they were composed. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Vedic literature existed in oral form for several centuries before it was written down.

questions.q: Write three questions you would ask when reading a hymn from the Rigveda as a historian.
questions.a: Where and when was it composed? What does it tell us about people's beliefs or occupations? What does it not tell us?
s: A question about time or place
A question about society or belief
A question about limits of the source

concepts.name: Political institutions: from janas to mahajanapadas and early kingdoms
concepts.description: Early Vedic clans and assemblies, the shift to territorial units, the sixteen mahajanapadas, the rise of Magadha and the Mauryas, and the early kingdoms of the south.
concepts.idea: Kin-based clans grew into territorial janapadas and mahajanapadas, and later into empires.
concepts.rule: Janas (clans) led by a raja; assemblies sabha, samiti, vidatha. Janapada (about 1000-600 BCE) is where a jana set its feet. Sixteen mahajanapadas; Magadha in Bihar most powerful. Rajyas and ganas/samghas. Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas (tiger, bow, fish) known from Sangam literature (300 BCE-300 CE).
concepts.example: The Rigveda names about thirty janas, five of which formed the panchajana.

questions.q: In early Vedic society janas were
questions.a: groups of people bound by kinship ties
o: groups of people bound by kinship ties

questions.q: The three assemblies mentioned in the Vedic texts are
questions.a: sabha, samiti and vidatha

questions.q: The most powerful mahajanapada, located in present-day Bihar, was ____.
questions.a: Magadha

questions.q: The emblem of the Cholas was
questions.a: the tiger

questions.q: In the Vedic period the raja was mainly
questions.a: a clan chief who led in warfare and protected the group
o: a clan chief who led in warfare and protected the group
an emperor over the whole subcontinent

questions.q: The term janapada means
questions.a: where a people first set its feet
o: where a people first set its feet

questions.q: Northern India had monarchical states called rajyas and republican states called
questions.a: ganas or samghas

questions.q: The Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas were known as
questions.a: the three crowned kings (Vendar) of Tamilakam
o: the three crowned kings (Vendar) of Tamilakam

questions.q: What change does the term janapada show about identity?
questions.a: It shows a shift from kinship-based identity to territorial identity, between about 1000 and 600 BCE, when people were tied to a land as well as to kin.

questions.q: The panchajana were
questions.a: five peoples: Yadu, Turvasha, Puru, Anu and Druhyu
o: five peoples: Yadu, Turvasha, Puru, Anu and Druhyu

questions.q: The Rigveda mentions about ____ janas.
questions.a: thirty

questions.q: Iron implements, a wider variety of grain and PGW pottery in the Ganga region in the first millennium BCE indicate
questions.a: growing agriculture and material culture

questions.q: Why did Magadha emerge as the most powerful mahajanapada?
questions.a: Its strategic location, fertile plains and strong rulers enabled it to expand control over neighbouring regions, leading to the Mauryan Empire.

questions.q: Name the southern polities and their emblems.
questions.a: Cholas (tiger), Cheras (bow) and Pandyas (fish).

questions.q: Trace the growth of political organisation from the Vedic period to the mahajanapadas.
questions.a: Vedic society was organised into kin-based janas led by a raja with assemblies. From about 1000 to 600 BCE janas settled as territorial janapadas. From about 600 BCE bigger mahajanapadas emerged, including monarchies and republics, and Magadha grew into the Mauryan Empire.

questions.q: The Satavahana Empire, which lasted nearly 500 years, succeeded the Mauryas in
questions.a: the Deccan

questions.q: How did the roles of the raja and the assemblies limit royal power in Vedic times?
questions.a: The raja led in war and protection, but the sabha, samiti and vidatha played a significant role in early governance, reflecting people's participation in decisions.

questions.q: What do we learn about early southern kingdoms from Sangam literature?
questions.a: The earliest Tamil literary tradition dating between 300 BCE and 300 CE describes the Chera, Chola and Pandya crowned kings, their rice-growing kingdoms, brave and ambitious kings such as a Chera ruler who earned the title adhiraja, and mentions Vedic yajnas and epic links.
s: Dates and nature of Sangam literature
Three crowned kings and fertile regions
An example of a king or link with Vedic tradition

questions.q: Meera says the early Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms are the same as the later imperial ones. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. The early kingdoms of Tamilakam (300 BCE-300 CE) should not be confused with the later imperial kingdoms.

questions.q: Make a timeline of five developments from the Vedic period to the Mauryas using the chapter.
questions.a: Janas and assemblies; janapadas around 1000-600 BCE; mahajanapadas from 600 BCE; rise of Magadha; the Mauryan Empire.

concepts.name: Ideas of kingship, governance and the pan-Indian ideal
concepts.description: Duties of a king, the seven constituents of the state, the ideal of a chakravarti ruler and the Junagadh Rock Inscription.
concepts.idea: Early texts saw the king as a protector who must ensure justice, and many rulers aspired to authority over the whole subcontinent.
concepts.rule: Arthashastra: seven constituents (saptanga): king, ministers, territory, forts, treasury, army, allies; "one wheel does not move the carriage". King protects and does justice. Terms Jambudvipa, Bharatavarsha, chakravarti kshetra express a pan-Indian ideal. Junagadh inscription has records of Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta.
concepts.example: Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda to commemorate his conquests along the Ganga.

questions.q: The seven constituents of the state (saptanga) are given in the
questions.a: Arthashastra

questions.q: According to the chapter the main duty of a king was
questions.a: to protect his subjects and ensure justice
o: to protect his subjects and ensure justice

questions.q: The Junagadh Rock Inscription is near Girnar in the state of ____.
questions.a: Gujarat

questions.q: The Arthashastra defines prithivi as
questions.a: the area between the Himavat and the sea
o: the area between the Himavat and the sea

questions.q: The seven constituents of the state include
questions.a: the king, ministers, territory, forts, treasury, army and allies
o: the king, ministers, territory, forts, treasury, army and allies
the priest, farmer, trader, soldier, teacher, poet and potter
the sun, moon, earth, air, fire, water and sky
the mandala, nadu, vishaya, bhoga, kottam, vithi and urs

questions.q: "One wheel does not move the carriage" means
questions.a: good governance needs cooperation and a well-organised administration
o: good governance needs cooperation and a well-organised administration

questions.q: Kingship was generally hereditary but there are references to kings being
questions.a: elected or expelled
o: ruling for life without change always

questions.q: Terms like Jambudvipa, Bharatavarsha and chakravarti kshetra show
questions.a: a pan-Indian geopolitical awareness

questions.q: What was the coronation oath in the Yajurveda?
questions.a: The king was advised to judge the strong and weak impartially and fairly, protect the country from calamities and do good to the people.
s: Protection and doing good to people

questions.q: The Chola ruler who took the title Gangaikonda was
questions.a: Rajendra I

questions.q: The Chera king Nedunjeral Adan won the rank of ____ (supreme king).
questions.a: adhiraja

questions.q: The Junagadh Rock Inscription is unique because it
questions.a: has records of three rulers from different periods
o: has records of three rulers from different periods

questions.q: Name the three rulers whose records appear on the Junagadh Rock and what each recorded.
questions.a: Ashoka (3rd century BCE) spread the message of Dhamma in Prakrit edicts; Rudradaman I (c. 150 CE) recorded his military achievements and repair of Sudarshana Lake in Sanskrit; Skandagupta (5th century CE) recorded restoration of the lake.

questions.q: Give two duties of a king as described in the Shanti Parva of the Mahabharata.
questions.a: To protect subjects from external threats and internal disorder, and to administer justice in cases such as abduction, robbery, theft and adultery.

questions.q: Explain the pan-Indian ideal of kingship with three examples from the chapter.
questions.a: Terms like Jambudvipa, Bharatavarsha, chakravarti kshetra express authority over the subcontinent. Ashoka spoke of Jambudvipa and the Arthashastra defines prithivi as between the Himalayas and the sea. The Chera king Nedunjeral Adan extended conquests to the Himalayas, and Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda.

questions.q: The state must have all seven constituents properly integrated because
questions.a: it can function effectively only if they work together
o: it can function effectively only if they work together

questions.q: Why did different rulers record their inscriptions on the same rock at Junagadh?
questions.a: The rock was already a public place of record and an important site associated with the Sudarshana Lake; adding to it linked their records and works to earlier rulers and showed continuity.

questions.q: Explain how the Arthashastra shows that governance was seen as a shared, organised effort.
questions.a: It describes the seven constituents of the state and says one wheel does not move the carriage, stressing cooperation and administrative machinery. It also says officers follow an energetic king and trains a king in governance.
s: King as example or training in governance

questions.q: Sam says early Indian kings had absolute and unlimited power. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Kings were bound by duties of justice and protection and, as texts show, could be elected or expelled, and assemblies took part in governance.
s: Gives evidence such as expulsion or duties

questions.q: Explain in your own words why it was important for rulers to protect people and ensure justice.
questions.a: Without protection and justice people would not trust the ruler, society would suffer disorder, and the state would not function or last; it made rulers accountable to their subjects.

concepts.name: Administration of kingdoms and empires and village self-government
concepts.description: Provincial and local administration, the Gupta system, decentralisation, the Pallava, Chalukya and Chola village assemblies and the Uttaramerur inscription.
concepts.idea: Empires were divided into provinces, districts and villages, and villages often governed themselves through assemblies.
concepts.rule: Kingdom → provinces (bhuktis in the north, mandalams in the south) → divisions → districts → villages. Gupta: mantri head of civil administration, sandhivigrahika minister of peace and war; district office of five members. Chola village assemblies did local work; Uttaramerur inscription describes the Kudavolai ballot pot system.
concepts.example: In the Kudavolai system a young child drew palm-leaf names from a pot in public to choose village representatives.

questions.q: Early Indian kingdoms were generally divided into
questions.a: provinces, divisions, districts and villages

questions.q: In the Gupta period the head of civil administration was the
questions.a: mantri

questions.q: The head of a village in the Satavahana empire was called the ____.
questions.a: gramika

questions.q: The Uttaramerur inscription of Parantaka I is located in
questions.a: Kanchipuram district of Tamil Nadu

questions.q: Between about 300 CE and 800 CE power was characterised by
questions.a: decentralisation, with provinces called bhuktis in the north and mandalams in the south
o: decentralisation, with provinces called bhuktis in the north and mandalams in the south

questions.q: District officers often consulted
questions.a: bankers, caravan leaders, artisans and scribes
o: bankers, caravan leaders, artisans and scribes

questions.q: A new officer introduced in the Gupta period was the
questions.a: sandhivigrahika, minister of peace and war
o: sandhivigrahika, minister of peace and war

questions.q: Village assemblies in the Chola empire
questions.a: were self-reliant and managed revenue, irrigation, roads and disputes
o: were self-reliant and managed revenue, irrigation, roads and disputes

questions.q: How did the village remain the smallest but important unit of administration?
questions.a: The village was the lowest unit, largely self-reliant and autonomous in infrastructure, social welfare and education, through assemblies and committees.

questions.q: The Damodarpur copper plates of Kumaragupta I record a district office of
questions.a: five members including a chief banker, caravan trader and artisan
o: five members including a chief banker, caravan trader and artisan

questions.q: The committees of village assemblies managing tasks like irrigation and temples were called ____.
questions.a: variyams

questions.q: The Pallavas made tax-free land grants to
questions.a: Brahmadeya villages

questions.q: Name the five members of the district office recorded in the Damodarpur plates.
questions.a: The head district officer, the chief banker, the chief caravan trader, the chief artisan and the chief of revenue collection.
s: All five named or correct roles

questions.q: Who were the three powers in the tri-partite struggle for Kannauj?
questions.a: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas and the Rashtrakutas.
s: All three named and Kannauj mentioned

questions.q: Describe the Kudavolai system of village elections at Uttaramerur.
questions.a: Names of eligible candidates were written on palm leaves and put in a large pot. In a public gathering, often at a temple, a young child drew the leaves one by one to choose representatives. The elected members were divided into committees (variyams) such as the tank committee.
s: Names on palm leaves in a pot
A child draws in public for fairness

questions.q: The Uttaramerur inscription says candidates should have
questions.a: "honest earnings" and be "pure" of mind

questions.q: How did dividing a kingdom into provinces, districts and villages help rulers?
questions.a: It let officers manage smaller areas, collect revenue and keep order, and let the ruler govern a large territory through a chain of local administrators.
s: Revenue or order across large territory

questions.q: Compare the administration of the Guptas and the imperial Cholas.
questions.a: Guptas kept the Arthashastra system with a mantri, added a minister of peace and war, kumaramatyas and district offices with local members. Cholas had mandalams, valanadus, nadus and urs, with village assemblies, committees and elections doing local administration.

questions.q: Ali says early Indian villages were completely controlled by the king and had no self-government. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Village assemblies and committees functioned as independent, self-reliant institutions in many kingdoms, as in Chola and Pallava times.

questions.q: Compare the administrative divisions of your state with the ancient divisions in the chapter and name two similarities.
questions.a: Both have provinces or states, districts and villages; both have officers at each level and local bodies like village councils or panchayats.

concepts.name: Ethics, dharma and the link between ethics and politics
concepts.description: The principles of samatva, rita and dharma and how ethics guided law, rulers and society.
concepts.idea: Indian thought grounded law and life in ethical ideas such as sameness, cosmic order and duty.
concepts.rule: Samatva: the principle of sameness. Rita: all-pervading cosmic order. Dharma: duty, righteousness (not religion), from the root dhri, meaning what upholds. Ashoka's dhamma stressed non-violence, compassion and respect in the family. The Uttaramerur inscription required honest earnings and a pure mind.
concepts.example: The dharma of iron is to sink and of wood is to float.

questions.q: Samatva is the principle of
questions.a: sameness

questions.q: In the Rigveda, rita is
questions.a: an all-pervading cosmic order representing harmony and balance
o: an all-pervading cosmic order representing harmony and balance

questions.q: Dharma is derived from the Sanskrit root ____.
questions.a: dhri

questions.q: The Pali equivalent of the Sanskrit word dharma is
questions.a: dhamma

questions.q: Here dharma refers to
questions.a: duty, obligation, righteousness and moral conduct
o: duty, obligation, righteousness and moral conduct

questions.q: According to samatva
questions.a: all bodies are made of the same matter and all consciousness is a manifestation of one supreme consciousness
o: all bodies are made of the same matter and all consciousness is a manifestation of one supreme consciousness

questions.q: Ashoka's edicts promoted dhamma by emphasising
questions.a: moral conduct, non-violence, compassion and respect in the family
o: moral conduct, non-violence, compassion and respect in the family

questions.q: Bhishma says dharma is
questions.a: "that which upholds beings"

questions.q: What does the saying "the dharma of iron is to sink and of wood is to float" mean?
questions.a: Dharma also means the law of existence, the nature of each thing; iron by its nature sinks and wood floats.
s: Dharma as the nature of a thing

questions.q: The epics criticise discrimination and present goodness as
questions.a: non-discriminatory

questions.q: The Rigveda describes the supreme consciousness as satya (true) and ____ (right).
questions.a: rita

questions.q: The Uttaramerur inscription is an example of ethics in governance because it
questions.a: required candidates to have honest earnings and be pure of mind
o: required candidates to have honest earnings and be pure of mind

questions.q: Give two examples of ethics and politics being linked in Indian history.
questions.a: Ashoka's edicts promoting dhamma, the Uttaramerur election rules for honest candidates, and works like Kamandaka's Nitisara and Kadambari that advise on kingship.

questions.q: What is the difference between dharma and religion in the chapter?
questions.a: Dharma here means duty, obligation, righteousness and moral conduct, ways of life guided by ethical values, not religion in the sense of a faith.
s: Dharma means duty and moral conduct
It is not the same as religion

questions.q: Explain how the principle of samatva is reflected in the epics.
questions.a: The Mahabharata includes characters of all varnas who, despite differences, uphold samatva. The epics criticise discrimination, present goodness as non-discriminatory and describe an ideal person or ruler as one who works for all.

questions.q: Why is the connection between ethics and politics important according to the chapter?
questions.a: Ethics form the basis of law and life and guided both state and society
o: Ethics form the basis of law and life and guided both state and society
Ethics have no link to law

questions.q: How does rita relate to human society?
questions.a: Rita is a cosmic order regulating nature that also upholds moral values, and represents the underlying order that maintains balance in the universe and in human society.

questions.q: Explain how dharma guided the life of individuals and rulers.
questions.a: Dharma required each person to perform their duties according to role and responsibilities, and students to respect parents, teachers and gods. For rulers it meant protecting people and doing justice; Ashoka's dhamma edicts show it in governance.

questions.q: Tara says dharma in the chapter means only religious rituals. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Dharma means duty, obligation, righteousness and moral conduct, guiding ethical life, and it also includes the nature of things.

questions.q: Write a short paragraph on how dharma can guide a student today.
questions.a: A student performs duties to parents and teachers, works honestly and regularly, respects others and helps the community, which is following dharma as duty and moral conduct.

concepts.name: Society: varna, jati, family, stages of life and the position of women
concepts.description: Varna and jati, social mobility, the family, the four ashramas and purusharthas, and women in early Indian society.
concepts.idea: Early social identity was flexible and occupation-based; varna was a functional division and jati grew later.
concepts.rule: The four varnas first appear in the Purushasukta of the Rigveda. Varna was functional; jati emerged from intermarriage, migrations and territorial differences and has no fixed number. Four ashramas: brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha, samnyasa. Purusharthas: dharma, artha, kama, moksha.
concepts.example: A Rigveda verse describes one family with several occupations, showing flexible occupations.

questions.q: The earliest reference to the four varnas is in the
questions.a: Purushasukta of the Rigveda

questions.q: The four ashramas are
questions.a: brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha and samnyasa

questions.q: The four goals of life (purusharthas) are dharma, artha, kama and ____.
questions.a: moksha

questions.q: The smallest and most basic social unit in Vedic society was the
questions.a: kula

questions.q: Varna was mainly
questions.a: a functional division based on roles
o: a functional division based on roles
a fixed division by birth from the start

questions.q: The number of varnas was fixed at four, while the number of jatis
questions.a: kept growing with new groups and occupations
o: kept growing with new groups and occupations

questions.q: A gotra is
questions.a: a patrilineal lineage traced to a common ancestor, often a Vedic sage
o: a patrilineal lineage traced to a common ancestor, often a Vedic sage

questions.q: The Rigveda verse about a family with different occupations shows that
questions.a: occupations were flexible and not strictly hereditary
o: occupations were flexible and not strictly hereditary
all family members had the same job

questions.q: How did the Sutta Nipata explain who is a brahmana?
questions.a: It says no one is a brahmana by birth, nor an outcaste by birth, but by deeds; a brahmana is such by his deeds.
s: Applies to both brahmana and outcaste

questions.q: Which jati-forming factor is mentioned in the chapter?
questions.a: intermarriage among varnas

questions.q: In Vedic society a group of grāmas formed the next larger unit, the ____.
questions.a: vish

questions.q: The Mandsaur Stone Inscription (473 CE) mentions
questions.a: a guild of silk weavers who migrated from Lata to Dashapura
o: a guild of silk weavers who migrated from Lata to Dashapura

questions.q: Name the four varnas and one traditional role of each.
questions.a: Brahmanas: study, teach and officiate yajnas. Kshatriyas (Rajanya): warfare, protection and justice. Vaishyas: agriculture, pastoralism and trade. Shudras: assist the other varnas (though also engaged in many economic activities).

questions.q: Name two women sages of the Rigveda and two women of the Sangam or Chola period.
questions.a: Apala, Vishvavara, Ghosha and Lopamudra were women sages. Avvaiyar and Vennikuyattiyar were Sangam women, and Sembiyan Mahadevi was a Chola queen supporting temple building.
s: Two women of the Sangam or Chola period

questions.q: Explain the four ashramas and the four purusharthas.
questions.a: Ashramas: brahmacharya (studentship), grihastha (householder), vanaprastha (forest life) and samnyasa (renunciation). Purusharthas: dharma (righteousness), artha (material well-being), kama (fulfilment of desires) and moksha (liberation). Artha should be pursued guided by dharma.

questions.q: The Tolkappiyam refers to a division of society into
questions.a: Arasar (kings), Vanigar (traders), Velar (farmers) and Antanar (brahmanas)

questions.q: What evidence shows social mobility in early India?
questions.a: Rulers such as the Nandas, Mauryas, Shungas, Satavahanas and Vakatakas came from diverse backgrounds, and the Mandsaur inscription shows a weavers' guild taking up other occupations after migrating.

questions.q: Explain how jati emerged and how it differs from varna.
questions.a: Jati emerged from factors such as intermarriage among varnas, migrating communities becoming endogamous and territorial differences. Varna is fixed at four functional categories while jatis have no limit and multiply as new groups and occupations arise.
s: Factors for the emergence of jati

questions.q: Nita says women in early India had no role in learning or public life. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Women took part in learning and rituals, attended the sabha, composed hymns (Apala, Ghosha and others) and later ruled or supported temples, though their position fluctuated over time.

questions.q: Write a short note on how the four ashramas prepare a person for life, giving one duty in each stage.
questions.a: Brahmacharya: study and discipline. Grihastha: run the household and earn. Vanaprastha: gradually withdraw and guide others. Samnyasa: renounce worldly ties for spiritual life.
s: Says they bring balance in life

concepts.name: Religious life, Bhakti, education and knowledge traditions
concepts.description: Vedic religion and worship of nature, renunciant traditions, the emergence of Bhakti, the gurukula and the centres of higher learning.
concepts.idea: Religion, education and learning in early India were tied to nature, ethics and a strong tradition of knowledge.
concepts.rule: Vedic deities linked to nature, worshipped through yajnas. Renunciants (parivrajaka, bhikshu, shramana). Bhakti with the Alvars (12, Vishnu) and Nayanmars (63, Shiva) in the 6th century Tamil region. Education was holistic under the guru-shishya tradition in the gurukula; centres such as Takshashila and Vikramshila.
concepts.example: Sun worship during Chhath and Makar Sankranti continues some ancient practices.

questions.q: Vedic deities were mostly associated with
questions.a: elements of nature such as the sun, rain and fire
o: elements of nature such as the sun, rain and fire

questions.q: Yajnas involved making offerings to
questions.a: the sacred fire

questions.q: The twelve saint-poets who praised Lord Vishnu were called ____.
questions.a: Alvars

questions.q: The sixty-three Shaiva saint-poets of the Tamil region were the
questions.a: Nayanmars

questions.q: The Vedic worldview showed
questions.a: respect and responsibility towards nature, seen as sacred
o: respect and responsibility towards nature, seen as sacred

questions.q: Bhakti offered
questions.a: a direct connection with the gods without elaborate rituals, open to all regardless of class or gender
o: a direct connection with the gods without elaborate rituals, open to all regardless of class or gender

questions.q: Renunciants of the first millennium BCE were called
questions.a: parivrajaka, bhikshu or shramana

questions.q: The guru in the gurukula was seen as
questions.a: a guide who led the student from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge
o: a guide who led the student from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge

questions.q: Why did education in early India emphasise both knowledge and moral values?
questions.a: It aimed at holistic preparation for life, cultivating truth, patience, humility, control of senses and reverence for all beings, and training pupils to live by dharma, with good character seen as the foundation of learning.

questions.q: Which subjects did students study according to the chapter?
questions.a: Vedas, grammar, logic, mathematics, medicine and astronomy
o: Vedas, grammar, logic, mathematics, medicine and astronomy

questions.q: The relationship between teacher and student is called the guru-____ paramparā.
questions.a: shishya

questions.q: Which institution is named as a major centre of higher learning in early India?
questions.a: Takshashila

questions.q: Name two practical skills and two arts or physical disciplines taught in early Indian education.
questions.a: Practical subjects include mathematics, medicine, science and astronomy; arts and crafts include music, dance, painting, physical education and martial arts such as archery, with yoga and meditation.
s: Two arts or physical disciplines named

questions.q: Which Tamil works are named as part of India's knowledge and literary traditions?
questions.a: Tiruvalluvar's Tirukkural, the epics Silappadikaram and Manimekalai, and the Sangam texts covering love (akam) and war or public life (puram).

questions.q: Describe life in a gurukula.
questions.a: The teacher's home was the centre of the gurukula, and the student was treated as a member of the teacher's family. Students lived a disciplined life of self-control, obedience and devotion, studied many subjects, practised yoga and meditation and served the guru.

questions.q: The Bhakti tradition gained prominence in the 6th century in
questions.a: the Tamil region

questions.q: How did renunciation relate to the Vedic tradition?
questions.a: The idea was already present in the Vedic tradition, since among the four ashramas vanaprastha and samnyasa are renunciatory. Around the middle of the first millennium BCE renunciants such as Buddha and Mahavira became influential.
s: Renunciants in the first millennium BCE

questions.q: Compare school life today with life in a gurukula, giving one advantage and one challenge of each.
questions.a: Gurukula: close guru-student bond and holistic training, but strict, residential discipline. Modern school: wider subjects and peers, but larger classes and less personal guidance.

questions.q: Ravi says Bhakti was only for the upper classes. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Bhakti was accessible to all, regardless of class or gender, with a direct connection to the gods without elaborate rituals.
s: Says it was open to all

questions.q: Write a short note on how a festival like Chhath or Makar Sankranti reflects the Vedic worldview.
questions.a: Both involve sun worship, reflecting the early respect for nature as sacred, dependence on it for survival and responsibility towards it.
s: Sacred and responsible view of nature

concepts.name: The economy: agriculture, irrigation, trade and guilds
concepts.description: Agriculture and land revenue, irrigation works, trade routes and ports, guilds and crafts in early India.
concepts.idea: Agriculture supported the state, and the growth of trade and guilds made the economy prosperous.
concepts.rule: Land tax was generally one-sixth of the produce (Mauryas). Irrigation: Sudarshana Lake dam (Pushyagupta), Chola tanks and the Grand Anicut (Kallanai). Trade routes Dakshinapatha and Uttarapatha; ports Muziris, Kaveripattinam, Arikamedu. Guilds (shrenis) regulated quality and prices, acted as banks, and metallic coins began with silver punch-marked coins.
concepts.example: The Nashik cave inscription records 3000 kahapanas invested in weavers' guilds.

questions.q: Agriculture in early India was
questions.a: the backbone of the economy

questions.q: The basic tax on land under the Mauryas was generally
questions.a: one-sixth of the produce

questions.q: Associations of traders and artisans in early India were called ____ (shrenis).
questions.a: guilds

questions.q: The two major land trade routes that emerged by the 6th century BCE were
questions.a: Dakshinapatha and Uttarapatha

questions.q: The Junagadh inscription records that Pushyagupta, a governor of Chandragupta Maurya,
questions.a: built a dam on Sudarshana Lake
o: built a dam on Sudarshana Lake

questions.q: The Grand Anicut (Kallanai), built by Karikala Chola,
questions.a: is still in use today

questions.q: The state ensured trade by
questions.a: keeping trade routes safe and preventing adulteration of goods
o: keeping trade routes safe and preventing adulteration of goods

questions.q: Guilds were important because they
questions.a: regulated quality and prices, supervised members through guild courts and acted as banks
o: regulated quality and prices, supervised members through guild courts and acted as banks

questions.q: Why did the state care about irrigation?
questions.a: Agriculture depended on irrigation and was a major source of revenue, so building and maintaining dams, canals and reservoirs was a preoccupation of the state.
s: It was a major source of revenue

questions.q: Which port is named among the important ports of early India?
questions.a: Muziris

questions.q: Deccan black soil was suited to the cultivation of ____.
questions.a: cotton

questions.q: The Milindapanho describes
questions.a: eight stages of agricultural operations

questions.q: Name two commodities Magadha traded, according to the Arthashastra, and one regulated by the state.
questions.a: Magadha traded textiles, gems, coral, pearls, metals and minerals. Salt production was strictly regulated by the state.

questions.q: What did the Sanchi inscription tell about guilds?
questions.a: The guild of ivory workers from Vidisha carried out welfare activities and carved the stone sculptures on the stupa gateways and railings, showing craft guilds took part in art and religious patronage.

questions.q: Describe irrigation works and their importance in early India.
questions.a: The Mauryan governor Pushyagupta built a dam on Sudarshana Lake near Girnar. The Cholas built canals, lakes and tanks; the Grand Anicut by Karikala Chola stored and distributed water, supported farming and settlements and is still used today.
s: Chola irrigation works and Grand Anicut

questions.q: Trade links between the Harappans and the Mesopotamians used
questions.a: ports along the western coast, the Persian Gulf and other regions
o: ports along the western coast, the Persian Gulf and other regions

questions.q: How did guilds act as banks?
questions.a: They received deposits from donors, invested funds and paid interest, as in the Nashik inscription where 3000 kahapanas were invested in weavers' guilds, so they functioned as financial and credit institutions.
s: Paid interest, with the Nashik example

questions.q: Explain how trade and guilds contributed to economic growth in early India.
questions.a: Well-structured states provided infrastructure and safe routes. Land routes and ports linked regions and reached Rome. Guilds regulated quality and prices, financed trade and crafts, and metallic coins circulated. Textile centres and craft guilds grew.
s: Coins or crafts and textile centres

questions.q: Meera says trade in early India was only local. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Trade routes, ports and sea lanes linked regions of the subcontinent and extended overseas; by the early centuries CE India had extensive trade with Rome.

questions.q: Suggest how a merchant in the Gupta period would benefit from belonging to a guild.
questions.a: The guild would maintain standards and fair prices, settle disputes in guild courts, help with loans and deposits, and support the merchant in trade over long distances.
